However, the next red line is placed at `00:33:434` (about 4 beats later), so the 5th beat of the previous section and the 1st beat of the new red line trigger within milliseconds of each other.\n\n---\n\n### How to Fix It\n\n#### 1. Check the Time Signature at `00:31:558`\nBetween `00:31:558` and `00:33:434`:\n$$\\Delta t \u003d 33,434 - 31,558 \u003d 1,876\\text{ ms}$$\nAt ~128 BPM, one beat is $\\approx 468.75\\text{ ms}$.\n$$1,876\\text{ ms} \\div 468.75\\text{ ms} \\approx 4\\text{ beats}$$\n\n* **Fix:** Change the time signature at `00:31:558` from **5/4** to **4/4**.\n\n---\n\n#### 2.       "text": "When changing the entire measure’s BPM ruins the snapping for notes in the middle of that bar, it means **the band rushed the first few beats and slowed down / dragged right before the downbeat** (very common in live human drumming).\n\nTo keep the previous 3 notes perfectly snapped *without* getting a double tick or overlapping barlines at the next section, use **split/subdivided timing**:\n\n---\n\n### The Solution: Split the Measure\n\nInstead of forcing one average BPM across the whole bar, split the bar into two timing sections:\n1. **Beats 1 to 3** (keeps the faster tempo so your 3 notes stay snapped).\n2. **Beat 4** (a 1-beat transition bar that absorbs the drag into the next downbeat).\n\n---\n\n### Step-by-Step Setup\n\n#### **1. Ranking Criteria:\n* **The #1 priority for timing is that objects land accurately on the audio transients.**\n* Live-recorded songs (like J-Rock/Indie bands) have natural human drift, rushed fills, and dragged downbeats.\n* BNs prefer you use split measures / micro-BPM adjustments rather than forcing a single BPM that causes notes to be 15–20 ms off-beat.\n\n---\n\n### 2.       "text": "**No, the teal line is too early.** \n\nHere is why, and where you actually want to align it:\n\n---\n\n### 1. How osu! Hitsounds Work\n* In osu!, hitsounds trigger **instantly** (0 ms delay) the moment a note is clicked or the tick is hit.\n* Hitsounds do **not** have a long pre-attack phase. \n\nIf your timing line is placed at the **teal line** (in the dead space before the audio), the hitsound will play *before* the drum in the song even makes a sound. When playing, this creates an audible \"flam\" (a sloppy double-tap sound) where the hitsound feels distinctly early.\n\n---\n\n### 2. What to Actually Align To: The Transient Onset\nYou want the timing tick to align with the **initial onset (rising edge)** of the drum waveform:\n\n```text\nSilence          Onset / Rising Edge (Target)\n───────           /│\\/\\/\\/\\\n─────────────────/ │ \\/\\/\\/\\  (Peak)\n                 ↑\n        [Place Timing Here]\n```\n\n* In your screenshot, the **white line** is positioned right where the drum waveform begins its sharp rise (the onset).\n* **The white line is where your timing should be.**\n\n---\n\n### 3. Quick Rule of Thumb\n* **Never place timing in the flat/silent zone** just to give room for a hitsound.\n* **Match the tick to the onset** (where the waveform first starts spiking). \n* To verify, play at **25% or 50% speed with the metronome enabled**: the metronome tick should click *at the exact same split-second* the drum hits, not before it.",

      "text": "**No, you definitely should not do this for the whole song.** \n\nWhat is happening here is called **\"over-timing\"** (or red-line spam), and it will cause serious issues for both gameplay and rankability.\n\n---\n\n### Why this is a major issue\n\n1. **Broken Bar Structure \u0026 Metronome**\n   * Notice that every single red line is set to **`4/4`**, but you are placing them every **1 to 3 beats**.\n   * This resets the downbeat constantly, meaning the game thinks a new musical measure starts every 1 or 3 beats. This completely breaks the 4/4 structure of the song.\n\n2. **Broken Mods \u0026 Visual Glitches**\n   * Mods like **Nightcore** will stutter erratically on every red line.\n   * Visual barlines in Standard, Taiko, and Mania will look chaotic and flash multiple times per second.\n   * Hitsound volumes and green lines (inherited points) will be extremely difficult to manage.\n\n3. **Ranking Criteria (RC) Violation**\n   * osu! RC rule: *\"Uninherited timing points must only be used where there is an actual, audible tempo change. Excessive or unnecessary timing points must be avoided.\"*\n   * BNs will disqualify a map that has alternating 123 $\\to$ 130 $\\to$ 123 $\\to$ 128 BPM red lines every single beat.\n\n---\n\n### Why Human Micro-Variations Don\u0027t Need Red Lines\nIn rock and band music, real drummers naturally fluctuate by **$\\pm5\\text{ to }15\\text{ ms}$** between individual kicks and snares. \n\n* In osu!, the **Hit Window (OD 8–9)** gives players $\\approx \\pm25\\text{ to }40\\text{ ms}$ of leniency.\n* Trying to chase every single micro-swing with red lines makes the editor timeline look \"perfect\", but makes the map feel jittery and unnatural to play.\n\n---\n\n### How You Should Actually Time This Song\n\n1. **Use One Constant BPM for Whole Phrases (4, 8, or 16 measures):**\n   * Set **128.00 BPM** (or the song\u0027s true base tempo) at the beginning of a section (e.g., start of Verse 1).\n   * Let that single red line run for the entire 8- or 16-bar phrase.\n\n2. **Only Add a Red Line When:**\n   * There is a clear tempo shift (e.g., the chorus speeds up).\n   * Cumulative drift causes the drum downbeat to wander **more than $\\approx 15\\text{–}20\\text{ ms}$ away** from the white grid line over several measures.\n   * A transitional fill drops or adds beats (e.g., a real $3/4$ or $2/4$ bar).\n\n3. **Rule of Thumb:**\n   If the song stays around 128 BPM throughout the verse, **one red line at the start of the verse** is usually all you need.",

If the metronome stays in groove with the snare and kick across 8–16 bars, you\u0027re done for that section.\n3. **Only Adjust at Structural Boundaries:** If the song naturally drifts or speeds up going into a chorus/solo, drop a single new red line on the **first downbeat (Beat 1)** of that new section.\n4. **Trust the Player\u0027s Hit Window (OD):** Minor human swing ($\\pm5\\text{–}10\\text{ ms}$) is part of the song\u0027s natural feel and is easily absorbed by the game\u0027s hit leniency.\n\nKeep your timeline clean with as few red lines as possible, and mapping the actual notes will be ten times easier and much smoother to play!",
